title: Kakutani Fixed Point Theorem (Constructive Content)
description: Formalizes the constructive content of Kakutani's theorem: an effective algorithm for approximating fixed points of correspondences. Proves the key Discrete IVT lemma and localization theorem, connecting to Scarf's pivoting algorithm (1967).

meta.author: researcher-2
meta.assumptions: 1 axiom (scarf_approx_fixed_point — Scarf's n-dimensional algorithm via Sperner's lemma, with full proof sketch). 0 sorries.
originalContributions: discrete_ivt_real: Discrete IVT for ℝ (PROVED by induction)
constructive_localization: O(n) grid search localizes fixed point (PROVED)
constructive_content_summary: Main theorem combining all results (PROVED)

overview.historicalContext: The question of whether Kakutani's fixed point theorem has constructive content was resolved by Herbert Scarf in 1967. While Brouwer's theorem and its generalizations (Kakutani, Schauder, Fan-Glicksberg) are classically non-constructive existence results, Scarf showed that the proof can be made algorithmic via Sperner's lemma on simplicial subdivisions. His pivoting algorithm finds ε-approximate fixed points in finitely many steps, with complexity O(n^2/ε^n). This established fixed point theory as a foundation for computational economics and game theory, leading to the development of computable general equilibrium models.
overview.problemStatement: Open Question OQ-04-OQ-04: Can the constructive content of Kakutani's fixed point theorem be extracted? Is there an effective algorithm that, given an upper hemicontinuous correspondence F : K → 2^K on a compact convex K ⊆ ℝⁿ and ε > 0, produces an ε-approximate fixed point of F in finitely many steps?
overview.proofStrategy: The formalization provides a complete YES answer for the 1D case and an axiomatized YES for the n-dimensional case: (1) Define ε-approximate fixed points and their basic properties. (2) Prove the Discrete IVT: for g : ℕ → ℝ with g(0) ≥ 0 and g(N) ≤ 0, find consecutive i, i+1 with sign change — in O(N) time. (3) Apply Discrete IVT to g(k) = F.upper(k/n) - k/n to localize the fixed point to a cell [i/n, (i+1)/n]. (4) Apply IVT to the crossing cell for an exact fixed point. (5) Axiomatize the Scarf algorithm for n-dimensions using Sperner's lemma.
keyInsights: **Discrete IVT as engine**: The sign change at a grid point is the finite, computable certificate of where the fixed point lives. This is the constructive heart of ALL fixed point algorithms.
**Localization vs. existence**: Constructive algorithms localize the fixed point to a cell; classical IVT/Kakutani then finds the exact point within that cell. The two steps are cleanly separated.
**Scarf = Sperner**: The Scarf algorithm is exactly the n-dimensional analogue of the 1D discrete IVT, with Sperner's lemma replacing the sign-change argument.
**Complexity trade-off**: The discrete grid search runs in O(1/ε) for 1D (O(1/ε^n) for nD), while IVT/Kakutani gives the exact point. Doubling n reduces error by half (bisection).

The constructive algorithm's complexity bound n=⌈2/ε⌉ achieving ε-accuracy connects to computational economics: Scarf's algorithm computes Nash equilibria and general equilibria in finite games by finding approximate fixed points, making the discrete IVT the algorithmic bridge from existence theorems to computable solutions.

sections.title: Module Header and Algorithm Description
sections.summary: Module docstring (1-58) documenting all 6 main results, the 1D constructive algorithm (Steps 1-6), connection to Scarf (Steps 1-6 generalizing to n-D), and references. Imports (60-67) and blank line before namespace.
sections.mathContext: Documents the equivalence: ε-fixed point algorithm (discrete IVT localization + IVT exactness) ↔ Scarf's pivoting (Sperner's lemma labeling). The docstring explicitly gives the algorithm: set n=⌈2/ε⌉, evaluate g(k)=u(k/n)-k/n, apply sign-change search, apply IVT.

sections.title: Part I: ε-Approximate Fixed Points
sections.summary: Namespace declaration, open. Defines IsApproxFixedPoint and HasApproxFixedPointProperty. Proves exact_implies_approx (exact → ε-fixed for all ε) and approx_fp_mono (ε-fixed → δ-fixed for δ ≥ ε).
sections.mathContext: An ε-approximate fixed point bridges constructive (finite-precision output) and classical (exact existence) fixed point theories. Monotonicity is trivial but essential for connecting approximation sequences.

sections.title: Part II: Discrete Intermediate Value Theorem
sections.summary: Proves discrete_ivt_real by strong induction on N: if g : ℕ → ℝ satisfies g(0) ≥ 0 and g(N) ≤ 0, there exist consecutive i < N with g(i) ≥ 0 and g(i+1) ≤ 0 (O(N) search). Also proves discrete_sign_change (product g(i)·g(i+1) ≤ 0 formulation).
sections.mathContext: The discrete IVT is the constructive analogue of the continuous IVT: a FINITE certificate (consecutive sign change) replaces the non-constructive existence claim. The induction structure mirrors bisection search.

sections.title: Part III: Constructive Fixed Point Localization
sections.summary: Applies discrete IVT to g(k) = F.upper(k/n) - k/n at n+1 grid points. Proves constructive_localization (crossing cell [i/n,(i+1)/n] in O(n) evaluations), exact_fp_from_localization (exact fixed point via kakutani_1d on cell), and approx_fp_property (HasApproxFixedPointProperty).
sections.mathContext: Boundary conditions: g(0) = u(0) - 0 ≥ 0 (upper bound ≥ 0 on [0,1]) and g(n) = u(1) - 1 ≤ 0 (upper bound ≤ 1). Discrete IVT gives crossing cell in O(n) steps. IVT on crossing cell gives exact fixed point.

sections.title: Part IV: Scarf Algorithm (n-Dimensional)
sections.summary: Extensive docstring explaining Scarf's 4-step algorithm (subdivision, Kakutani labeling, Sperner's lemma, ε-fixed centroid) with O(n²/εⁿ) complexity. Axiom scarf_approx_fixed_point for UHC correspondences on compact convex K ⊆ ℝⁿ, and scarf_approx_fp_property (its corollary).
sections.mathContext: Scarf's labeling L(v) = argmin_i(v_i - (y_v)_i) satisfies the Sperner boundary condition: vertices on face σ_S (coordinates in S are on boundary) get labels in S. Sperner's lemma then gives a completely labeled simplex.

sections.title: Part V: Limit Theorem and Computational Complexity
sections.summary: Proves seq_compact_Icc ([0,1] is sequentially compact). Proves approx_fp_limit_1d (ε_n → 0 fixed points accumulate at exact fixed point, fully proved via LSC/USC continuity of F.lower/F.upper). Proves bisection_complexity (n = ⌈2/ε⌉ achieves ε-precision).
sections.mathContext: The limit theorem uses sequential compactness to extract x_{φ(n)} → x*, then uses continuity of F.lower and F.upper (via continuousWithinAt) to show F.lower(x*) ≤ x* ≤ F.upper(x*). Complexity: n = ⌈2/ε⌉ gives error 2/n < ε.

sections.title: Part VI: Summary Theorem and Status Table
sections.summary: constructive_content_summary: combines (a) O(n) constructive localization, (b) exact fixed point existence (kakutani_1d), and (c) O(1/ε) complexity guarantee. Status table documenting all results. End of namespace KakutaniConstructive and final status markdown.
sections.mathContext: The constructive content packages three assertions: finite algorithm (localization), classical existence (Kakutani), and complexity bound (bisection). Together they answer OQ-04-OQ-04: YES, Kakutani has extractable constructive content.

conclusion.summary: The formalization answers YES to OQ-04-OQ-04: the constructive content of Kakutani's theorem can be extracted. 12 theorems fully proved, 1 axiom (Scarf algorithm, suitable for proving from Sperner's lemma). The key result discrete_ivt_real is the constructive engine for all fixed point algorithms.
conclusion.implications: This provides the algorithmic foundation for computable fixed point theory: Scarf's algorithm computes Nash equilibria in finite games, general equilibria in Arrow-Debreu models, and solutions to fixed point problems in game theory and economics. The discrete IVT is the finite analog of the IVT that makes computation possible.
openQuestions: Can the scarf_approx_fixed_point axiom be proved from Sperner's lemma (proved in the gallery) via the Kakutani labeling construction? This would make the formalization fully axiom-free and close the constructive content of Kakutani's theorem.
Can the Scarf algorithm's O(n²/εⁿ) complexity bound be proved formally in Lean, tracking the number of pivoting steps needed to find a completely labeled simplex?
Can the limit theorem (approx_fp_limit_1d) be extended to n-dimensional UHC correspondences, giving a full passage from ε-approximate to exact fixed points in the Scarf setting?

crossReferences.description: Kakutani's theorem (OQ-04) is the set-valued generalization of Brouwer. This formalization provides its constructive content.
Nash equilibrium existence (OQ-04-OQ-01) uses Kakutani; the Scarf algorithm can compute Nash equilibria.
Infinite-dimensional Kakutani (OQ-04-OQ-03); Scarf's algorithm extends to locally convex spaces via Fan-Glicksberg.
BrouwerOQ02 proves the contraction mapping theorem with O(log 1/ε) complexity. Scarf's algorithm achieves O(1/εⁿ) for the more general UHC case.
